explanation: South African dung beetles roll their balls in a straight line, away from rivals. Fitted with tiny caps that hid the sky, they wandered; under a planetarium Milky Way, they kept course.

claims.text: Experiments in South Africa showed that dung beetles can steer by the Milky Way when the Moon is not visible.
Fireflies, crickets and cockroaches have not been shown to navigate by the Milky Way.
Dung beetles roll their dung balls in a straight line away from the dung pile, which helps them avoid competitors.
In experiments, dung beetles fitted with caps that blocked their view of the sky could not hold a straight course.
Under a planetarium sky showing the Milky Way's band of light, dung beetles kept a straight course.

evidence.restatement: Dacke and colleagues (2013) showed that South African dung beetles orient by the Milky Way on moonless nights.
No such Milky Way navigation has been shown for fireflies, crickets or cockroaches.
Dung beetles roll their balls in a straight line away from the dung pile, escaping competitors.
Beetles fitted with caps that blocked their view of the sky could not hold a straight course.
In a planetarium showing only the Milky Way's band of light, the beetles still held a straight course.
